takeaways: A December tour of Pulte's Mercer model at Meadow View Preserve, a new south-metro development with many lots available at the time: about 2,700 square feet with four bedrooms upstairs, priced around the mid-$600,000s.

The main floor has an entry office nook, a large matte-finish island with a black sink, double ovens, a gas fireplace (which can heat the home if the furnace fails, unlike many electric units) with stacked stone and slat accent walls, dining for eight, a second work nook and a mudroom bench.

Upstairs are a large laundry room with cabinets, an owner's suite with ceiling speakers, a tiled shower, a semi-private water closet and a closet with a window, plus three more bedrooms and a hall bath with double sinks.
The unfinished basement has 9-foot ceilings and corner mechanicals; finishing it (family room, bath and an egress bedroom) runs about $40,000 to $45,000, according to the video.

faq.q: Is a gas fireplace better than an electric one?
faq.a: A gas fireplace can heat much of a home if the furnace fails, while many electric units are mostly decorative, Jason notes. Gas also adds real warmth on cold Minnesota nights.

takeaways: The steps to selling a Twin Cities home. Step 1: talk with an agent, who gathers details about your home's condition and planned updates and prepares a comparative market analysis.
Step 2: meet at the home to review pricing, marketing and commission, with no commitment either way. Step 3: sign a listing agreement that sets out pricing and both sides' obligations.
Research agents first: look for 50-plus reviews on Google or Zillow. Jason notes the average agent sells about five homes a year.
In a shifting market, don't cut the price too soon. If comparable homes take about 60 days to sell, reducing after 15 days gives away money unnecessarily.

After an offer: the agent confirms the buyer's pre-approval, then you work through inspection, appraisal and title. Sellers can often sign closing documents ahead of time instead of attending the closing.

faq.q: What are the steps to selling a house in Minnesota?
faq.a: Get a market analysis, meet with your agent to set price and strategy, sign a listing agreement, market the home, accept an offer, complete inspection, appraisal and title work, then close. Sellers can often pre-sign closing documents.

faq.q: When should I lower my asking price?
faq.a: Compare your days on market with similar homes. If comparable homes have been taking about 60 days to sell, cutting your price after two weeks is usually premature.

takeaways: Jason and Brooke Huerkamp share low-cost ways to prepare a home's interior for sale. Buyers want move-in ready, so fixing things beats offering a credit; like a dirty truck on the lot, a home that needs work gets mentally discounted.

1: declutter and depersonalize. Start packing early, remove family photos and clear about half of what's in closets and cupboards. Store boxes in a pod or the garage, leaving room to park at least one car.
2: paint in fresh, neutral colors and fix nicks. Materials for a 3,000-square-foot home run under about $1,000; a painter costs roughly $6,000 to $7,500, and the return is usually worth it.
3: focus on kitchens and baths: deep clean, update dated fixtures and cabinet pulls, and add new towels, shower curtains and bedding you'd buy for your next home anyway.

4: flooring: restretch loose carpet (Jason paid about $400 for seven areas), refinish hardwood floors, or replace worn flooring with luxury vinyl plank. The team has preferred vendors and interior designers to help.

faq.q: Should I offer a credit instead of painting before selling?
faq.a: Usually not. Buyers respond to a move-in-ready first impression and tend to discount a home that needs work by more than the credit. Fresh, neutral paint often pays for itself.

faq.q: What's the cheapest way to get my house ready to sell?
faq.a: Declutter and depersonalize first, then paint in neutral colors, deep clean the kitchen and baths, and restretch or refresh flooring where needed.

takeaways: Jason talks with Jess of Goosehead Insurance about what drives homeowners insurance premiums. Location matters: some carriers won't write policies in certain counties, and flood zones and local crime affect price.

Fire protection matters a lot on rural property: carriers look for a hydrant within about 1,000 feet and a fire station within about 5 miles. On a roughly $1 million home, she's seen premiums around $5,600 a year inside those limits versus about $13,000 outside.

Your insurance score reflects your claims history; even calling to ask about a claim can be recorded. Water damage from maintenance issues (like a failed sump pump) hurts most; storms count less. Small claims can raise premiums for three to five years, so consider paying minor repairs yourself.

The house itself: carriers want roofs about 10 years old or newer, may refuse aging cedar shake roofs, and often won't cover knob-and-tube wiring. Wood or coal stoves as a secondary heat source add risk.

Deductibles are rising: higher deductibles lower premiums, and separate wind and hail deductibles of about 1% of dwelling coverage (about $5,000 on a $500,000 home) are now common. Minnesota has been a loss state for insurers in recent years, largely because of hail.
Be upfront about short-term rentals, certain dog breeds, trampolines, pools and hot tubs. Specialized coverage exists, and hiding them can void a claim.

faq.q: Why are homeowners insurance rates rising in Minnesota?
faq.a: Largely hail. Minnesota has been a loss state for insurers in recent years, so carriers are raising premiums and deductibles and adding separate wind and hail deductibles, often about 1% of dwelling coverage.

faq.q: Should I file a small homeowners insurance claim?
faq.a: Often not. Claims stay on your record for three to five years and can raise premiums or affect coverage, so paying for small repairs yourself can save money over time.

faq.q: Does the age of my roof affect home insurance?
faq.a: Yes. Many carriers want roofs about 10 years old or newer and may limit or deny coverage on older roofs, especially aging cedar shake.
